newsitem.title: IRAQ: Turkish foray displaces civilians in northern Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Turkish foray displaces civilians in northern Iraq.

text.p: The Turkish military incursion into northern Iraq is displacing civilian Kurds and increasing tension in the area, Iraq's U.N. coordinator said on Wednesday.

Shrugging off international criticism of its military foray in pursuit of Turkish Kurd guerrillas, Turkey has been pouring more men, supplies and weapons into the region to bolster its campaign which started last Wednesday.
"We have noted that the military operations have produced movement of people and increased tension among civilians," Iraq's U.N. coordinator Steffan de Mistura told Reuters.
He did not say how many civilians were displaced but said United Nations agencies and guards in the area were still assessing the situation.
"When there is bombing and shelling people try to leave the scene," de Mistura said.
He said the military operations did not provide a suitable environment to implement Iraq's oil-for-food deal with the United Nations which went into effect in December.
"We have been concerned about the Turkish military incursion in northern Iraq because any type of military activity does provide a disruption of humanitarian activity," he said.

Under the deal Iraq is allowed to export $2 billion worth of oil in six months to buy urgent humanitarian needs for its population suffering from trade sanctions imposed by the United Nations for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

About $260 million of the nearly $1.3 billion remaining for Iraq, after deducting 30 per cent for a 1991 Gulf War reparations fund and defraying other U.N. costs, are earmarked for Kurds living in the three northern provinces of Dohuk, Arbil and Sulaimaniya currently outside the control of the central government.
The distribution of supplies in the Kurdish region is solely in U.N. hands. De Mistura said his guards and relief workers were unable to reach areas where shelling and bombing took place.
But he said the Turks and their Kurdish allies were not obstructing the flow of convoys carrying items under the deal and were not barring U.N. guards and relief workers from entering the area.
The United Nations has so far distributed wheat flour, rice, pulses and other items among the Kurds.
In their sweep, the Turks are aided by the local militia of Kurdish warlord Massoud Barzani, head of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP).
"(Resolution) 986 needs a proper environment to be properly implemented," de Mistura said of the Security Council resolution on which the oil-for-food deal is based.
"We have noted that the Turks have been very careful not to stop 986 vehicles...We have not noticed any interference in the freedom of movement or distribution plans," he said.
